# Why does espresso taste bitter?

Bitterness in espresso usually comes from over-extraction. Hot water keeps pulling compounds out of the ground coffee, and the last compounds to dissolve are the harsh, drying ones. A shot that runs too long, a grind that is too fine, or water that is too hot can each push extraction past the point where the cup tastes sweet and balanced.

## What makes a shot run long?

A grind that is too fine slows the water down, so the shot takes longer and extracts more. Tamping very hard has a smaller effect than most people expect, but an uneven tamp lets water channel through one side of the puck, which over-extracts that side and under-extracts the rest.

Roasters also point at freshness. Beans that are only a few days past roasting release a lot of gas, which makes the flow uneven and can leave some of the coffee bed under-extracted while the rest goes bitter. Resting the beans for a week often evens out the flow and the taste.

## How do I fix a bitter shot at home?

Start by changing one thing at a time. Coarsen the grind slightly and pull another shot, then taste it next to the first one. If the shot still tastes harsh, shorten it by stopping the pump a little earlier, or lower the water temperature if your machine allows it.

Clean equipment matters as well. Old coffee oils build up on the group head and in the portafilter basket, and they turn rancid and bitter over time. A quick backflush and a wipe of the basket after each session keep those flavors out of the next cup.

Finally, check the milk. In a latte or a cappuccino, scorched milk can taste bitter even when the espresso itself is fine. Steam the milk until the jug is hot to the touch but still comfortable to hold, and the drink will taste sweeter without any change to the shot at all.
